worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as

$$
\int \frac{7}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-49}}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{7})}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic cosine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{7})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{7}.$ Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{7}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=7\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{7}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-49}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{7})}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot 7\,\text{d}u \\  & =7\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =7\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C \\  & =7\operatorname{arcosh}⁡(\frac{x}{7})+C\end{aligned}
$$
